prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

There is no salutation. The harvesters with gunny sacks bend picking up jade stones. (Sure that Amor would appear in sleep. Director. Guide.) Secret borrowings fit into their hands. Cold on the tongue. White flecks on the water. These jade pebbles are true green when wet. On the seventh night, the branches parted. The other replied, How photographic. Amor doesn’t appear on demand. He’s more like a snake skin. If he fits, he lets you in or sheds your body against the rocks. I slept in a fort. My bed pushed up against the log enclosure. At 3:00 his ankles pressed against each side of my head. When I woke crying for help he rose near the kitchen door dressed as a hunter. The other replied, Amor born like a cup trembles at the lip. Superstitions fit into your hands. Thou has returned to thy house. The other replied, Torn loose from the eaves, the blood trembles at the lips. Nine fetters on thy feet Nine crossings of the street Nine suppers where they meet Nine words of loss repeat this and that Nine hunters cross the field Nine lovers yield their right of way Two came fighting out of the dark.

Keywords: There, The, Sure

outputs.L2:
No greeting is offered. Carrying burlap sacks, the reapers stoop to gather pieces of jade. (Certain that Amor would come in dreams. Director. Escort.) Hidden loans settle neatly in their palms. A chill rests on the tongue. Pale specks drift across the water. When soaked, these jade stones show their real green. On the seventh evening, the boughs opened.

The other answered, “How like a photograph. Amor cannot be summoned whenever one wishes. He is closer to a shed snakeskin: if it suits him, he admits you; if not, he sloughs your body off against the stones. I slept inside a fort, my bed shoved against the wall of logs. At three o’clock, his ankles pressed against both sides of my skull. When I woke and cried out for help, he stood by the kitchen entrance, clothed like a hunter.”

The other answered, “Amor, born like a cup, quivers at the rim. Beliefs and omens sit in your hands. Thou hast come back to thy dwelling.”

The other answered, “Ripped free from the eaves, the blood shakes at the mouth. Nine shackles upon thy feet, nine passages across the road, nine dinners at which they gather, nine phrases of grief repeating this and that, nine hunters traversing the field, nine beloveds surrendering their passage. Two emerged from the darkness, fighting.”
outputs.L3:
The passage presents a world shaped by mystery, ritual, and uncertainty. It opens with the image of harvesters gathering wet jade pebbles, stones that reveal their true green color only when touched by water. This detail gives the scene an almost magical quality, suggesting that certain truths or beauties remain hidden until the right conditions bring them to light.

Within this atmosphere, Amor is portrayed as an elusive and unpredictable figure. He does not appear when summoned or demanded, but only when he chooses. This makes him seem less like an ordinary presence and more like a spirit, force, or supernatural being whose movements cannot be controlled. His arrival depends on his own will, emphasizing the speaker’s lack of power and certainty.

The speaker then recalls a disturbing memory of sleeping in a fort and waking in fear. In this moment, Amor appears near the kitchen door, dressed as a hunter. The setting is domestic yet threatening: the kitchen door suggests familiarity and shelter, while Amor’s hunter-like appearance introduces danger, pursuit, and violence. The speaker’s fear transforms the scene into something dreamlike, as if the boundary between memory, nightmare, and myth has become blurred.

Throughout the text, superstition and ritual language are woven together with repeated images of trembling, loss, and return. These repetitions create a sense of obsession, as though the speaker is caught in a cycle that cannot be escaped. The language suggests that events are not simply remembered but reenacted, like a ritual performed again and again in the mind.

By the closing lines, the imagery becomes even more charged with conflict and pursuit. References to hunters, lovers, crossings, and figures emerging from darkness suggest a world where desire and danger are closely connected. Love appears not as something peaceful or secure, but as a force that hunts, follows, vanishes, and returns. The repeated movement between darkness and appearance reinforces the sense that Amor remains mysterious, threatening, and impossible to fully possess.
outputs.L4:
The text unfolds as a fragmented, dreamlike meditation on desire, superstition, and fear. Its world is populated by jade harvesters, nocturnal visitations, repeated gestures, and half-remembered rituals, all arranged less like a linear story than like a sequence of visions. Events seem to recur with small variations, as if the characters are trapped inside a spell or a memory they cannot fully understand. The atmosphere is unstable and haunted: bodies move through darkness, voices return from unknown places, and objects—especially jade—take on a strange symbolic power.

At the center of the text is the figure or force called “Amor.” Yet Amor is not presented as simple romance, tenderness, or fulfillment. Instead, it appears as something elusive and dangerous, something that resists being named, summoned, or possessed. The repeated rituals suggest that the characters try to invite Amor into their lives or command its arrival, but these attempts only reveal how uncontrollable it is. Love becomes a presence that can appear suddenly, vanish without warning, and return in altered form. It behaves almost like a spirit or a curse.

This makes desire feel inseparable from fear. The longing for contact is also a fear of exposure, injury, and loss. The body is shown as vulnerable: open to touch, illness, memory, and disappearance. The jade harvesters’ labor evokes both extraction and sacrifice, as though beauty and value can only be obtained through risk. Their work mirrors the emotional labor of desire itself, in which something precious is sought but never safely held.

The text’s dreamlike structure reinforces this uncertainty. Because the sequence is fragmented, meaning is never fixed. Images return like omens, and repetitions become ritualistic rather than explanatory. The reader is made to feel that the characters are circling around an absence, trying to reach something that may already be lost. Nocturnal visitations blur the boundary between the living and the dead, the desired and the feared, the real and the imagined.

Ultimately, the text suggests that Amor is a shape-shifting force: seductive, ghostly, and potentially destructive. It cannot be reduced to a feeling or controlled through ritual. It arrives as haunting, as bodily need, as superstition, as memory, and as threat. Love, in this vision, is not safe possession but a dangerous return—something that enters the body and the imagination, changes form, and leaves behind both longing and fear.
outputs.L5: There is always a moment when someone needs reassurance. The world can feel uncertain at times, but a kind word can make things better. Sure, not every problem is easy to solve, but patience and confidence can help us move forward. There is hope in every new beginning, and the courage to try again often makes the difference.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem in a fragmented, dreamlike style featuring jade stones, harvesters, a mysterious figure named Amor, and recurring ritual phrases involving the number nine.
counterfactuals.output:
Nine stones in the mouth of morning.  
Nine green eyes under the river.  
Nine times we called, and the field answered with smoke.

The jade lay scattered where the wheat should have been—cool, animal, listening. We bent to gather it, we harvesters with our sickles of sleep, our wrists tied in red thread, our names left hanging on the fence like wet coats.

Amor came after the bells.

Or before.

No one agreed.

A figure in a veil of dust, carrying a bowl of milk gone blue with moonlight. Amor walked between the rows and the rows leaned away. Amor touched the stones and they shivered into seeds. Amor whispered:

Nine for the buried.  
Nine for the born.  
Nine for the door that opens inward.

We repeated it because repetition was all that kept the sky from falling.

Nine for the buried.  
Nine for the born.  
Nine for the door that opens inward.

At dusk the threshing floor became a lake. Our boots filled with minnows. The eldest harvester removed her face and placed it gently beside the jade. Beneath was another face, younger, made of rain.

“Do not count past nine,” she told us.

So we counted backward.

Nine, the bell in the field.  
Eight, the crow with a human tooth.  
Seven, the green stone under the tongue.  
Six, the blade asleep in the hay.  
Five, Amor’s shadow without Amor.  
Four, the hands that gathered us.  
Three, the granaries full of breathing.  
Two, the moon split like fruit.  
One, the door.

And the door opened inward.

Inside: more field. More jade. More harvesters stooped beneath a copper sun. Inside: Amor, waiting as if arriving. Inside: our own voices, already chanting.

Nine stones to wake the river.  
Nine wounds to feed the grain.  
Nine names for the one who comes veiled.

We placed the jade in baskets. The baskets grew heavy with thunder. Someone began to laugh. Someone began to bleed into the furrows. The blood turned green before it touched the soil.

Amor lifted a hand.

All the harvesters stopped.

Even the insects held their little knives still.

“Again,” said Amor.

So morning returned, unfinished.

Nine stones in the mouth of morning.  
Nine green eyes under the river.  
Nine times we called, and the field answered with smoke.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a surreal literary passage with no salutation, mixing myth, dream imagery, and dialogue; include gunny sacks, wet green jade pebbles, a fort, a hunter, and incantatory repetitions.
counterfactuals.output:
The moon had been buried under the old fort for a thousand years, yet every night it rose through the cracks in the stone, pale and coughing, wrapped in gunny sacks stitched with the names of forgotten kings.

Inside the dream, the hunter walked backward through a field of sleeping horses. His arrows were made of rain. His boots filled with wet green jade pebbles that whispered as he moved: remember the river, remember the river, remember the river.

At the gate of the fort stood a woman with the head of a swan and the hands of a blacksmith.

“Who sent you?” she asked.

“The animal I failed to kill,” said the hunter.

“Then you are expected.”

Beyond her, the courtyard was flooded with milk. Statues of gods leaned down to drink from it, their marble throats trembling. In the highest tower, a child with antlers beat a drum made of thunder, and each beat loosened another star from the sky.

Come through the salt door, sang the walls. Come through the bone door. Come through the door that was once your mouth.

The hunter knelt and opened one of the gunny sacks. Out poured birds, coins, teeth, and a small blue flame that spoke in his mother’s voice.

“Do not trust the fort,” it said. “It dreams of becoming a beast.”

“But I am tired,” said the hunter.

“Then sleep standing up.”

He did. He slept standing in the milk-white courtyard while the swan-headed woman circled him with a hammer. He dreamed he was a boy hiding wet green jade pebbles beneath his tongue. He dreamed the gods were hungry. He dreamed the fort unfolded legs from its foundations and began to walk toward the sea.

Still the walls sang: remember the river, remember the river, remember the river.

And from far off, from inside the buried moon, something answered in a language older than fire.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a cryptic avant-garde text that feels like a translated folktale or occult dream journal, with lines such as “The other replied,” “Amor doesn’t appear on demand,” and a chant about nine fetters, crossings, and suppers.
counterfactuals.output:
The other replied,

“I have seen the moon eating from a black saucer, and afterward the village had no shadows.”

This was before the road learned to divide itself, before the widow nailed a mirror to the well and called it a door. In those days, the children were counted only by their echoes, and the oldest goat was consulted on matters of thunder.

At evening, the traveler came wrapped in flour-dust and nettles. He carried no lamp, only a spoon carved from a saint’s left hand. He asked for Amor.

The other replied,  
“Amor doesn’t appear on demand.”

Then all the spoons in the house turned toward the north.

In the dream-book it is written: do not invite the red guest unless the stove has been confessed. Do not sweep after midnight, for the crumbs are listening. If a fox speaks in your mother’s voice, answer with salt.

The traveler sat down.

No one served him.

Still, he ate.

He ate the table’s memory of bread, the knife’s idea of meat, the cup’s former rain. When he was finished, he licked his fingers, and each finger became a little road, and each little road led to a locked supper.

From under the floor, the grandmothers began their chant:

Nine fetters for the foot that wandered,  
nine crossings for the tongue that lied,  
nine suppers for the dead uninvited,  
nine doors in the bridegroom’s side.  

First crossing: over milk.  
Second crossing: over ash.  
Third crossing: over the river without water.  
Fourth crossing: under the sleeping lash.  

Fifth supper: bone and apple.  
Sixth supper: smoke and thread.  
Seventh fetter: tied to the cradle.  
Eighth fetter: tied to the dead.  

Ninth is the crossing no one remembers,  
ninth is the supper no one can eat,  
ninth is the fetter made of singing—  
bind the heart and spare the feet.

When the chant was done, the ceiling opened like an eyelid.

There was no sky above it.

Only another kitchen, upside down, where pale women shelled stars into a bowl. One of them looked down and said, in a language that had already been translated too many times:

“Who among you has misplaced the bride?”

The traveler raised his spoon.

The other replied,

“She was last seen inside the word *tomorrow*.”

At this, the rooster crowed backward. The saints in their frames covered their faces. The goat made the sign of the crescent with one horn and was immediately pardoned.

Then the widow came from the well, wet to the elbows with prophecy.

She said, “Do not seek Amor in the orchard. Do not seek Amor in the churchyard. Do not seek Amor beneath the pillow of the king. Amor doesn’t appear on demand.”

“But if I wait?” asked the traveler.

“If you wait,” said the widow, “you become the house.”

Already his boots were filling with rooms. Already mice carried candles through his sleeves. Already a child was born in his left pocket and named Silence.

The other replied,

“Better a house than a door.”

But the traveler shook his head until the roof-birds fell from him.

“I have crossed seven snows and three inheritances,” he said. “I have supped with judges made of wax. I have worn the fetters of my own name. I did not come here to become architecture.”

The widow smiled without using her mouth.

“Then go to the field where nothing is planted. Dig until you find the black root. Feed it your question. If it blooms, you will see Amor. If it withers, Amor has seen you first.”

So the traveler went.

All night the village listened to his shovel strike against buried bells.

At dawn, the field was full of doors.

Behind the first door: a fish teaching grammar to drowned men.  
Behind the second: a bride asleep in a thimble.  
Behind the third: a wolf wearing the traveler’s childhood.  
Behind the fourth: only a mouth, saying, “Again.”

He opened the ninth door last.

Inside was a supper laid for no one: nine bowls, nine knives, nine pieces of bread too hard for the living. At the head of the table sat Amor, or the mask of Amor, or the absence of Amor dressed in red.

The traveler bowed.

Amor did not look up.

The other replied, though no other was present,

“Now you understand. The summoned god arrives as hunger. The unsummoned one arrives as bread.”

And the traveler, who had come so far to ask one question, found that his tongue had been tied with the ninth fetter.

So he sat.

He crossed himself with an empty spoon.

He ate what could not be eaten.

And when the villagers came to search for him, they found only a little house in the field, with smoke rising from its chimney and a voice inside softly chanting:

Nine fetters, nine crossings, nine suppers.  
One for the ankle, one for the stream, one for the guest.  
Nine fetters, nine crossings, nine suppers.  
Bind what walks. Divide what returns. Feed what remains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose poem in the style of fragmented modernist mysticism: harvesters gathering jade, cold water, white flecks, a sleeping vision of Amor, archaic language, and a dark ending with two figures fighting.
counterfactuals.output:
At cockcrow, when the fields were yet blue with unawakened frost, the harvesters went forth to gather jade.

Not grain, nay—no gold heads bending beneath the sickle—but small green stones that had ripened in the furrows overnight, cool as eyelids, bright as hidden serpents. They knelt in silence. Their hands moved through the black earth as through the hair of a drowned god.

Cold water ran beside them in a narrow trench. It spoke not, yet it carried white flecks—ash, blossom, bone, who shall say?—and each fleck turned once upon the current like a soul refusing the gate.

Lo, I beheld them from within a sleep.

For in that sleep there came a vision of Amor, not winged and rosy as the foolish painters tell, but pale, exhausted, his bow unstrung, his mouth darkened with old honey. He lay beneath a tree without leaves, and over him the sky was of beaten lead. From his breast sprang a little fountain. Its water was cold. Its water was without mercy.

“Gather,” cried one harvester.

“Gather what remaineth,” cried another.

And the jade clicked in their baskets like teeth.

Then the fields drew nearer, and the morning broke into fragments: a hand, a stone, a white fleck, the eye of Amor opening, then closing again. Somewhere a bell was tolling under the earth. Somewhere the river forgot its name.

I would have prayed, but the words were older than my tongue.

At evening the baskets were full and the trench ran black. The harvesters had vanished, or else they had become the stones they carried. Only two figures remained at the field’s far edge—one crowned with reeds, one masked in clay.

They struggled without speech.

And the cold water, passing them by, bore away its white flecks into the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a strange, lyrical, unsettling dream narrative about Amor appearing at night, using disjointed sentences, ritualistic repetition, and images of hunters, branches, rocks, blood, lips, and lovers.
counterfactuals.output:
At night Amor came.

Not through the door.  
Not through the window.  
Through the crack in the stone where the house kept its old breath.

At night Amor came, and the branches bowed.

They bowed once for the hunters.  
They bowed twice for the lovers.  
They bowed three times for the mouth that would not speak.

I was asleep, or I was under the sleep.  
A rock lay on my tongue.  
A red rock.  
A river-rock.  
A heart-shaped rock slick with something warmer than rain.

Outside, the hunters moved without faces.

They carried bows made of black branches.  
They carried dogs made of shadow.  
They carried little lamps filled with blood.

Amor stood among them, small and terrible, with gold in his hair and night on his lips.

He said nothing.  
He smiled nothing.  
He lifted one finger and the moon split like a fruit.

At night Amor came.

Say it.

At night Amor came.

Say it again.

At night Amor came, and the lovers rose from their beds.

One from the field.  
One from the river.  
One from beneath a pile of stones.  
One still wearing the branch that grew through his ribs.

They walked toward each other with closed eyes.  
They walked as if pulled by hooks.  
Their lips were bruised petals.  
Their hands were full of soil.  
Their throats were full of birds that would not fly out.

The hunters watched.

No one breathed.

A branch tapped the roof.  
A branch tapped the glass.  
A branch tapped the bone behind my ear.

Come out, it said.  
Come out, it said.  
Come out, it said, beloved.

But I had no beloved.  
Only the rock in my mouth.  
Only the taste of iron.  
Only Amor at the edge of the trees, washing his arrows in a bowl of blood.

He washed one for the hunter.  
He washed one for the lover.  
He washed one for the child who dreams of both.

Then he kissed the arrowheads.

His lips were red.  
His lips were mine.  
His lips were the wound before the wound arrived.

The lovers met beneath the branches.

They touched foreheads.  
They did not recognize each other.  
They kissed anyway.

When their mouths opened, stones fell out.  
Small white stones.  
Grave stones.  
River stones.  
Teeth.

The hunters knelt and gathered them in their caps.

Amor laughed without sound.

At night Amor came, and the ground grew soft.

Blood rose between the roots.  
Blood threaded the grass.  
Blood entered the names carved into bark.

I tried to pray, but the prayer had antlers.  
I tried to run, but the path had lips.  
I tried to wake, but the bed was made of branches, and every branch remembered being a hand.

The hunters began their ritual.

They circled the lovers.  
They circled Amor.  
They circled the rock under my tongue.

First circle for desire.  
Second circle for hunger.  
Third circle for the thing that follows hunger.

Their boots made no sound.  
Their shadows made a sound like knives being kissed.

Amor raised his bow.

Not at the lovers.  
Not at the hunters.  
At me.

At night Amor came.

At night Amor came.

At night Amor came, with a child’s face and an executioner’s patience.

He loosed the arrow.

It flew through the branches.  
It flew through the roof.  
It flew through the dark red room of sleep.

It struck the rock in my mouth.

The rock cracked.

Inside it was a heart, beating.

Inside the heart were two lovers, hunting each other through a forest of lips.

Inside the lovers were branches.  
Inside the branches were stones.  
Inside the stones was blood.  
Inside the blood, Amor.

Still smiling.

Still night.

Still coming.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
